derivations.claim: Since $|\mathbf n|=1$, $P=I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ satisfies $P^*=P=P^2$ and is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbf n^\perp$; writing $z=Pz+\mathbf n(\mathbf n\cdot z)$ gives $\|Pz\|^2=\|z\|^2-|\mathbf n\cdot z|^2$, so $\|P\|\le1$. Write $C_{\mathbf n}v=\mathbf n\times v$, whose matrix is real skew-symmetric. Expanding with $\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{\ell m k}=\delta_{i\ell}\delta_{jm}-\delta_{im}\delta_{j\ell}$ gives $(C_{\mathbf n}^2v)_i=n_i(\mathbf n\cdot v)-v_i=-[P(\mathbf n)v]_i$. Antisymmetry also gives $\mathbf n\cdot C_{\mathbf n}v=0$ and $C_{\mathbf n}\mathbf n=0$, so $PC_{\mathbf n}=C_{\mathbf n}P=C_{\mathbf n}$. Consequently $h(\mathbf n)^*=h(\mathbf n)$, $h(\mathbf n)^2=P(\mathbf n)$, and $Ph=hP=h$.
Applying the polar-coordinate formula in [F3] to the density $(2r)^{-1}$ gives $d\nu=(r/2)\,dr\,d\Omega$. Orthogonal maps preserve $d\Omega$ by [F4] and fix $r$, so they preserve $\nu$.

Applying [F3] to the radial density $(2r)^{-1}$ gives
$$\nu(\{r_0\le|\mathbf k|\le r_1\})=\frac12\int_{r_0}^{r_1}r\,dr\int_{S^2}d\Omega=\pi(r_1^2-r_0^2).$$
The annuli $\{1/m\le|\mathbf k|\le m\}$ have finite measure and cover $M$, so $\nu$ is sigma-finite.

Given $f\in\mathcal H_T^\nu$, put $u=Wf\in\mathcal H_T^0$ by [F1]. Write $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$. For each of the three components, [F2] and [A1] give a compactly supported smooth $v_j$ with $\|u_j-v_j\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}<\varepsilon/(3\sqrt3)$. The three component choices are permitted by Countable Choice, and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ then satisfies $\|u-v\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}<\varepsilon/3$.

For each $m$, [F5] supplies a smooth cutoff $\rho_m$ equal to $1$ on $\overline B_{1/m}(0)$ and supported in $B_{2/m}(0)$; set $\chi_m=1-\rho_m$. By [F3], $\lambda_3(B_{2/m}(0))=4\pi\int_0^{2/m}r^2\,dr=(4\pi/3)(2/m)^3$. Since $v$ is bounded,
$$\|\chi_m v-v\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}\le\|v\|_\infty\sqrt{\lambda_3(B_{2/m}(0))}\longrightarrow0.$$
Choose $m$ large enough that this norm is below $2\varepsilon/3$. The field $\chi_m v$ is smooth, compactly supported away from $0$, and can therefore be projected with the smooth matrix $P(\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|)$.

The operators $P_\sigma$ are self-adjoint and
$$P_\sigma^2=\frac{P+2\sigma h+h^2}{4}=P_\sigma,\qquad P_+P_-=0,\qquad P_++P_-=P.$$
Moreover $hP_\sigma=\sigma P_\sigma$. The trace of $P$ is $2$ and the trace of $h=iC_{\mathbf n}$ is $0$, so $\operatorname{tr}P_\sigma=1$; a finite-dimensional orthogonal projection has rank equal to its trace, hence each range is a complex line.

The matrices $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)$ depend smoothly on $\mathbf n$. For any $\mathbf n_0$, choose $v\in\mathbb C^3$ with $P_\sigma(\mathbf n_0)v\ne0$. Continuity makes $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)v$ nonzero on a neighborhood of $\mathbf n_0$, and normalizing this smooth vector gives a smooth unit local section. Thus the ranges form the stated smooth line subbundles.

Set $g_m(\mathbf k)=P(\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|)\chi_m(\mathbf k)v(\mathbf k)$. It is smooth, transverse, and compactly supported away from $0$. Since $Pu=u$ for the transverse field $u$ and $\|P(\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|)\|\le1$ by step 1.1,
$$\|g_m-u\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}\le\|\chi_m v-v\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}+\|v-u\|_{L^2(d^3\mathbf k)}.$$
The choices in steps 1.4 and 1.5 make the right side less than $\varepsilon$. The inverse image $W^{-1}g_m=\sqrt{2|\mathbf k|}\,g_m$ is smooth and compactly supported away from $0$, hence belongs to $\mathcal D$. As $W$ is unitary by [F1], $\mathcal D$ is dense in $\mathcal H_T^\nu$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Put $M=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega(\mathbf k)=|\mathbf k|$, and $d
u(\mathbf k)=d^3\mathbf k/(2\omega(\mathbf k))$. Define the unit sphere by $S^2=\{\mathbf n\in\mathbb R^3:|\mathbf n|=1\}$ with the subspace topology. For $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$, chart $\{\varepsilon n_j>0\}$ by the other two coordinates in the open unit disk $B_1^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|<1\}$, with inverse $n_j=\varepsilon\sqrt{1-\sum_{i
e j}n_i^2}$; these six charts and their transition maps are smooth. Let $d\Omega$ denote polar surface measure on this sphere. Polar coordinates give $d
u=(r/2)\,dr\,d\Omega$, and every orthogonal map preserves $
u$. The transverse one-photon Hilbert space $\mathcal H_T^
u$ consists of the equivalence classes $f\in L^2(M,
u;\mathbb C^3)$ satisfying $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ for $
u$-almost every $\mathbf k$, with pairing $\langle f,gangle_
u=\int_M\overline{f(\mathbf k)}\cdot g(\mathbf k)\,d
u(\mathbf k)$, linear in $g$. The preceding measure-isometry lemma gives the unitary $Wf(\mathbf k)=f(\mathbf k)/\sqrt{2\omega(\mathbf k)}$ from this space to the transverse space defined with measure $d^3\mathbf k$. The null set $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted throughout.

For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, define $P(\mathbf n)=I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$. Extend the real cross product complex-linearly by $(\mathbf n	imes v)_i=\sum_{j,\ell=1}^3\epsilon_{ij\ell}n_jv_\ell$, where $\epsilon_{ij\ell}$ is totally antisymmetric and $\epsilon_{123}=1$, and set $h(\mathbf n)=i\,\mathbf n	imes$ and $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)=(P(\mathbf n)+\sigma h(\mathbf n))/2$ for $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$. Each $P_\sigma(\mathbf n)$ is a rank-one orthogonal projector on the complex transverse plane $P(\mathbf n)\mathbb C^3$, and $h$ has eigenvalue $\sigma$ on its range. The fibers $\mathcal L_{\sigma,\mathbf n}=\operatorname{ran}P_\sigma(\mathbf n)$ form smooth complex line subbundles of $S^2	imes\mathbb C^3$. Here a smooth line subbundle means a family of one-dimensional complex fibers with smooth local unit sections. The common smooth domain for differential calculations is

$$\mathcal D=\{f\in C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb C^3):\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0	ext{ for every }\mathbf k\in M\}.$$

It is dense in $\mathcal H_T^
u$. For $0<r_0<r_1<\infty$, the mass-shell measure of the radial annulus is $
u(\{r_0\le|\mathbf k|\le r_1\})=\pi(r_1^2-r_0^2)$; in particular $
u$ is sigma-finite.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], the Axiom of Choice [A1] supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of [F2]. Choose a measurable representative of $f$ and let $N\subset M$ be a $
u$-null set outside which $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$. Invariance of $
u$ gives $
u(RN)=0$. For $\mathbf k
otin RN$, $$\mathbf k\cdot Rf(R^{-1}\mathbf k)=(R^{-1}\mathbf k)\cdot f(R^{-1}\mathbf k)=0,$$ so $U(R)f$ is transverse almost everywhere. If the representative is changed on a null set $N'$, its rotated composition changes only on $RN'$, also null; hence $U(R)$ is well-defined on $L^2$ equivalence classes. Since $R$ preserves $d
u$ by [F2] and preserves the Hermitian norm on $\mathbb C^3$, change of variables gives $\|U(R)f\|_
u=\|f\|_
u$. The same formula with $R^{-1}$ is an inverse, so $U(R)$ is unitary.

On the Lebesgue transverse space write $U_0(R)u(\mathbf k)=Ru(R^{-1}\mathbf k)$. Since $|R^{-1}\mathbf k|=|\mathbf k|$, the multiplier $W$ satisfies $$W(U(R)f)(\mathbf k)=\frac{Rf(R^{-1}\mathbf k)}{\sqrt{2|\mathbf k|}}=R\frac{f(R^{-1}\mathbf k)}{\sqrt{2|R^{-1}\mathbf k|}}=U_0(R)(Wf)(\mathbf k).$$ Thus the weighted and Lebesgue rotation actions are unitarily intertwined.

For $R\in SO(3)$, $(R\mathbf n)\times(Rv)=R(\mathbf n\times v)$: pairing both sides with any real $w$ reduces the equality to invariance of the oriented scalar triple product under $R$. Hence $P(R\mathbf n)=RP(\mathbf n)R^{-1}$, $h(R\mathbf n)=Rh(\mathbf n)R^{-1}$, and $P_\sigma(R\mathbf n)=RP_\sigma(\mathbf n)R^{-1}$. Substituting $\mathbf n=R^{-1}\mathbf k/|R^{-1}\mathbf k|$ proves that the multiplication projector $P_\sigma$ commutes with $U(R)$.

Put $A=[\mathbf a]_\times$, so $A^T=-A$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|BC\|_F\le\|B\|_F\|C\|_F$, so $\|B^m/m!\|_F\le\|B\|_F^m/m!$ for every $m\ge1$; the $m=0$ term is $I$ with $\|I\|_F=\sqrt3$. Hence the matrix-exponential series converges absolutely. For $B=tA$ the same estimate gives uniform convergence on bounded $t$-intervals; its Cauchy product and the binomial identity give $R_{\mathbf a}(s)R_{\mathbf a}(t)=R_{\mathbf a}(s+t)$, while termwise transposition gives $R_{\mathbf a}(t)^T=R_{\mathbf a}(-t)$. Thus $R_{\mathbf a}(t)$ is orthogonal. It is continuous in $t$, so its determinant is the constant $1$ (it lies in $\{+1,-1\}$ and equals $1$ at $t=0$). Hence $R_{\mathbf a}(t)\in SO(3)$ and $t\mapsto R_{\mathbf a}(t)$ is a one-parameter subgroup. Termwise differentiation gives $R_{\mathbf a}'(0)=A$.

For $R_1,R_2\in SO(3)$, $R_1R_2$ is again orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $R^{-1}=R^T$. Hence $$U(R_1)U(R_2)f(\mathbf k)=R_1R_2f(R_2^{-1}R_1^{-1}\mathbf k)=U(R_1R_2)f(\mathbf k),$$ and $U(I)=I$, so $U$ is a unitary representation.

First let $f\in\mathcal D$ be nonzero. Its compact support is a compact subset of $M$, so [F6] applied to $\mathbf k\mapsto|\mathbf k|$ gives $0<r_0\le|\mathbf k|\le r_1<\infty$ on the support. Thus it lies in a radial annulus $K=\{r_0\le|\mathbf k|\le r_1\}$. The set $SO(3)	imes K$ is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space: the equations defining $SO(3)$ are closed and its matrix entries have absolute value at most $1$. Hence it is compact by [F4]. The map $(R,\mathbf k)\mapsto Rf(R^{-1}\mathbf k)$ is continuous there, so [F4] makes it uniformly continuous. Rotations preserve $K$ and $
u(K)<\infty$ by [F2]; therefore $R\mapsto U(R)f$ is continuous in $L^2(d
u)$. For $f=0$ this continuity is immediate. For general $f\in\mathcal H_T^
u$, choose $g\in\mathcal D$ with $\|f-g\|_
u<\varepsilon$ by [F2]. Unitarity gives $$\|U(R)f-U(R_0)f\|_
u\le2\varepsilon+\|U(R)g-U(R_0)g\|_
u,$$ so continuity on $\mathcal D$ extends to all $f$ as $R	o R_0$.

By steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2, and 1.4, $t\mapsto U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group. Applying Stone's theorem [F3] gives its unique self-adjoint generator $T_{\mathbf a}$ with $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{itT_{\mathbf a}}$. Set $J_{\mathbf a}=-\hbar T_{\mathbf a}$; then $J_{\mathbf a}$ is self-adjoint and $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{-itJ_{\mathbf a}/\hbar}$.

By step 1.4, $R_{\mathbf a}'(0)=[\mathbf a]_	imes$. For $f\in\mathcal D$, differentiating $G(t,\mathbf k)=R_{\mathbf a}(t)f(R_{\mathbf a}(-t)\mathbf k)$ at $t=0$ gives $\partial_tG(0,\mathbf k)=(\mathbf a	imes f)(\mathbf k)-(\mathbf a	imes\mathbf k)\cdot
abla_{\mathbf k}f(\mathbf k)$, which equals $- rac{i}{\hbar}(L_{\mathbf a}+S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}})f$ because $-iS_{\mathbf a}v=\mathbf a	imes v$. If $f
e0$, use the closed radial annulus $K$ from step 2.2 containing its compact support; for $t$ near zero each $G(t,\cdot)$ is supported in $K$. The product of a compact time interval and $K$ is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^4$, hence compact by [F4], and $G$ and its $t$-derivative are continuous there. Thus [F4] makes $\partial_tG$ uniformly continuous. For each fixed $\mathbf k\in K$ and each of the six real coordinate functions $g(s)$ of $G(s,\mathbf k)\in\mathbb C^3\cong\mathbb R^6$, set $m=(g(t)-g(0))/t$ for $t
e0$. The function $g(s)-ms$ has equal endpoint values on the compact interval between $0$ and $t$. If it is nonconstant, [F6] gives an interior maximum or minimum. Difference quotients from the two sides then have opposite weak signs, so differentiability forces its derivative there to be zero. If it is constant, its derivative is zero everywhere. Thus $m=g'(c)$ for some $c$ between $0$ and $t$. Uniform continuity and $|c|\le|t|$ imply that the difference quotients of $G$ converge uniformly on $K$ to $\partial_tG(0,\cdot)$. Since $
u(K)<\infty$ by [F2], this gives convergence in $L^2(d
u)$; the quotients lie in the closed subspace $\mathcal H_T^
u$ by step 1.1, so the limit is the norm derivative in that space. For $f=0$ the derivative is immediate. By the Stone derivative characterization in step 3.1, $f\in D(J_{\mathbf a})$ and $J_{\mathbf a}f=(L_{\mathbf a}+S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}})f$.

If $f\in\mathcal D$, then $(\mathbf a\times\mathbf k)\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf k\cdot f)=0$; expanding this derivative and using $\mathbf k\cdot f=0$ gives $\mathbf k\cdot L_{\mathbf a}f=i\hbar(\mathbf k\times f)\cdot\mathbf a$. The matrix definition of $S_{\mathbf a}$ gives $\mathbf k\cdot S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}}f=-i\hbar(\mathbf k\times f)\cdot\mathbf a$. Their sum is zero, so step 4.1 shows that $J_{\mathbf a}$ preserves transversality on $\mathcal D$.

The separate terms need not preserve transversality. For $\mathbf a=e_3$, choose by [F5] a smooth bump $\rho$ equal to $1$ on $B_{1/8}(0)$ and supported in $B_{1/4}(0)$, and translate it to $\chi(\mathbf k)=\rho(\mathbf k-e_1)$. Its support misses the $e_3$ axis. Put $f(\mathbf k)=\chi(\mathbf k)(e_3\times\mathbf k)$. Then $f\in\mathcal D$, while $(\mathbf k\times f)\cdot e_3=\chi(\mathbf k)(k_1^2+k_2^2)$ is nonzero near $e_1$. By the calculation in step 5.1, both $\mathbf k\cdot L_{e_3}f$ and $\mathbf k\cdot S_{e_3}^{\mathrm{op}}f$ are nonzero there, with opposite signs. This proves that neither term separately preserves the transverse space, whereas their sum does.
